lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Welcome to the sind course. Let's start with the big question: why run Slurm in Docker?
Picture this: you've just written a new job script, and you'd like to see it run before it meets the real cluster.
But on a production cluster, every quick test waits in the queue. And trying out a configuration change there puts everyone's jobs at risk.
Research software engineers want to test job scripts like yours. Admins want to rehearse a change before production gets it.
Developers want a real Slurm in their CI pipelines. And a trainer wants every participant in a course to get the same setup.
Whoever you are, you need the same thing: a real Slurm cluster that's quick to make, and safe to break.
Usually, the choices are the production queue, or dedicated machines and VMs that someone has to provision.
Tools like Vagrant and Docker Compose can get you there, but they demand real configuration effort, and maintenance.
First, a quick refresher. A Slurm cluster has a controller, running slurmctld, and compute nodes, each running slurmd.
You submit a job with sbatch or srun. It waits in the queue until a node is free, and then slurmd runs it.
Behind the scenes, munge vouches for every message, so the daemons can trust each other.
Now, the idea behind sind. Every Slurm node becomes its own Docker container, right on your machine.
Inside each one, systemd boots first, so munge, SSH and the Slurm daemons start just like on bare metal.
Its command line is modelled on kind, the Kubernetes in Docker tool. All you need is sind and Docker.
Need more? Add workers to a running cluster, or run several clusters side by side.
Let's see it in action. Run sind create cluster, and seconds later, a controller and a worker are up.
Behind it, sind creates a network and volumes, generates the munge key and slurm.conf, starts the node containers, and waits until they're all ready.
Then sind get nodes lists the node containers: one for the controller, and one for worker zero.
Each one has its own host name and IP address, just like a real machine.
Done testing? sind delete cluster, and it's gone.
Of course, there's a trade-off. sind gives up some flexibility, in return for ease of use and speed.
What you get back: every cluster starts clean and identical, for each person on your team and for every CI run.
It's a tool for development and testing, not a controller for production clusters. And that's exactly the point.
So, three things to remember. Every node is a container, with systemd inside.
One command creates a cluster, and one deletes it. And it's made for testing, from job scripts to CI.
Next up: your first cluster, from the install to your first job. See you there!
